#9365. Shanghai’s art week finds buyers in a selective market

Shanghai’s two leading art fairs, West Bund Art & Design and Art021, opened this week against a backdrop of slowing economic growth, subdued confidence in China’s art market and an increasingly crowded international art calendar. While the city no longer commands the same international panache it enjoyed before the pandemic, galleries report encouraging early sales, suggesting that committed collectors remain active despite a more cautious market.

“I think the serious people who have a long-term idea of what they want to do, they keep collecting,” says René Meile, director of Galerie Urs Meile, which has a location in Beijing. He adds that younger collectors increasingly favour artists of their own generation. While established artists continued to attract buyers, collectors were taking longer to commit to expensive works. Meile attributed the shift partly to the departure of speculative buyers from the market.

Meanwhile this year’s art week brings an explosion of art events city-wide and boasts many newcomers both in terms of industry visitors and new spaces, including three new galleries. Hangzhou’s longtime fair regular Inna Art Space just opened Inna Front Room in the Lujiazui business district, making it the first significant gallery on the Pudong side of the river. Chen Yongwei, the former director of nonprofit Pond Society, has opened Shanghai Industry atop the Suhe House art cluster. PTT Space, a rising star gallery from Taipei, meanwhile this week opened an outpost at the M50 gallery complex.

“Even though the Chinese market is at an all-time low, Shanghai is still a vibrant international city with many art institutions,” says Robert Hsu, who founded PTT in 2020. “Considering the past art week, the number of openings parties and fairs is still through the roof, surpassing Seoul Art Week and coming close to Hong Kong Art Week.”

Hsu says he also has existing “base infrastructure” in the city with staff and relationships with local artists and collectors. “As a second generation gallerist, I feel we have to keep moving in this new era. The market, the business, the people have all changed. To survive, I have to step out of our comfort zone and explore.”

Jae Pil Eun's Night Walking, showing at Hang Over

Courtesy of the artists and SYSTEMA © SYSTEMA, 2026

Along with the gallery, Hsu is part of the team organising the new boutique fair Art Fusion Canton in the southern Chinese city Guangzhou next month (3-7 December). In Shanghai, the popup fair Hang Over (11-15 November) is going strong in its second year. Moving from last year’s restaurant to an event space in a new lifestyle complex on Donghu Lu, it this year features 18 galleries including Tokyo’s Misako & Rosen, Seoul’s Cylinder along with Shanghai’s Antenna Space, Vanguard and Linseed, owned by Hang Over founder Zhuang Lingzhi.

The 13th edition of West Bund Art & Design (10–15 November) brought together 85 galleries, including Hauser & Wirth, Perrotin, Thaddaeus Ropac and White Cube. Meanwhile, the 14th Art021, hosting 111 galleries at the Shanghai Exhibition Centre, has introduced a new acquisition initiative with the Los Angeles County Museum of Art (Lacma), supported by Chinese collectors, aimed at bringing works by Asian and Asian diaspora artists into the museum’s collection.

At West Bund, Thaddaeus Ropac reports several opening-day sales, led by Megan Rooney’s That Sky (Atlas) (2026), sold for £400,000 to a Chinese foundation. Other transactions included a painting by Martha Jungwirth for €200,000, a Robert Longo work for $90,000 and a painting by Han Bing for €55,000, acquired by an Asian museum. A work by Joan Snyder was also sold to a Chinese museum.

Dawn Zhu, the gallery’s Asia director, praises the enthusiasm of collectors, noting that the gallery had made early sales to both institutions and private collections. “We are seeing collectors who have travelled from across South East Asia and even a few from Europe,” she says.

Hauser & Wirth also reports significant sales at West Bund, led by Louise Bourgeois’s bronze sculpture Point of Contact (1967–68, cast 2006), which sold for $450,000 to a museum in Kuala Lumpur. Other transactions include Lee Bul’s Perdu XXXIII (2020), sold for $260,000 to a private collection in China, and another Bourgeois work, Femme (2008), acquired by a Chinese private collector for $165,000. The gallery also reports the sale of George Condo’s Black and Red Composition (2026) for $200,000.

At Art021, Galerie Urs Meile reports sales of works by Xie Nanxing for approximately RMB 1.2m and Ju Ting for RMB 400,000, alongside works by younger artists Chen Zuo and Miao Miao priced between RMB 100,000 and RMB 150,000, and a smaller painting by Vietnamese artist Mai Ta for RMB 40,000.

Also at Art021, Shanghai-based gallery Bank reports strong early sales of Liang Hao’s works, priced 60,000 to 300,000 RMB, and of a large Jiang Cheng painting for over 500,000 RMB. The gallery reports that Lacma may acquire a video work made in 2000 by Los Angeles-based artist Patty Chang.

Despite the more subdued atmosphere, some galleries remain optimistic about the depth of China’s domestic market. Liang Xiao, a spokesperson for Perrotin, which has operated a Shanghai space since 2018, says that the slowdown had given collectors more time to select works they genuinely appreciate.

He suggests that the growth of new art fairs in Yokohama, Seoul and elsewhere would not fundamentally undermine Shanghai’s position, given the size of China’s domestic collector base. “Even after all these years, there are still many collectors we have yet to reach,” Liang says, adding that Shanghai remains an important entry point for collectors from across mainland China.

Hsu says the feedback for PTT Shanghai has been “quite positive” in the debut week, but “the market is not at its best.” Transactions have been slow, but included some successful placement of works with established collectors. “As the old saying goes, the gallery business is a marathon, not a sprint.”

Before comparing your balance to anyone else's, you need to know what the benchmarks actually include. Most retirement savings data from Vanguard, Fidelity, and the Federal Reserve covers:

What these numbers typically exclude: taxable brokerage accounts, real estate equity, HSA balances invested for retirement, pension values, and Social Security. For FI-minded savers, this distinction matters enormously — your total investable net worth is almost certainly larger than your "retirement savings" as defined by these surveys.

The gap between average and median retirement savings is one of the most important distinctions in personal finance. The average gets pulled upward by high-balance accounts — a single person with $5 million in their 401(k) dramatically inflates the average for their age group. The median (the middle number when all balances are ranked) gives you a far more honest picture of what a typical American actually has saved.

Notice how the gap widens with age. By 65+, the average is 3.3 times the median — meaning a small number of disciplined savers (or high earners) are pulling the average far above what most people actually have. The median tells you what a typical person in each age group actually holds. If you are above the median, you are doing better than half of Americans your age. But "better than average" and "on track for a secure retirement" are very different standards.

Vanguard's annual "How America Saves" report and Fidelity's quarterly retirement analysis provide the most comprehensive snapshots of what Americans hold in their workplace retirement accounts. These numbers reflect defined-contribution plan balances only — primarily 401(k) and 403(b) accounts.

Average balance: $13,265. Median balance: $5,400. Most savers in this bracket have been contributing for fewer than five years. The biggest advantage this group has is time — a 25-year-old contributing $6,000 per year with a 7% average return will accumulate over $1.2 million by age 65 without ever increasing their contribution. The FI community emphasizes that getting started early matters far more than starting with large contributions.

Average balance: $53,300. Median balance: $21,000. This is where employer matches start compounding meaningfully. Fidelity data shows that employees who have been contributing consistently since their 20s have balances 2.5 to 3 times higher than those who started in their 30s. The typical employer match adds 3-6% of salary — effectively free money that many employees still leave on the table. According to Vanguard, roughly 25% of eligible employees do not contribute enough to capture their full employer match.

Average balance: $142,069. Median balance: $60,763. Earnings typically peak in this decade, making it the critical window for aggressive savings. FIRE-path savers in this age bracket commonly have $500,000 to $1 million or more saved by maximizing their 401(k) ($25,500 in 2027), HSA ($4,500 individual / $9,000 family), and Roth IRA ($7,000) — then directing additional savings into taxable brokerage accounts.

Fidelity's guideline of 1x salary by 30 and 10x salary by 67 is a reasonable starting point for traditional retirement planning. But for FI seekers, these benchmarks are the floor, not the ceiling. The ChooseFI community consistently demonstrates that saving 40-60% of income — rather than the national average of 4.6% — compresses the timeline from 40 working years down to 10-17.

If your balance is below the median for your age group, you are not alone — and you are not stuck. The math of compound growth means that aggressive action in your 40s and 50s can still produce a secure retirement or even an early one.

The IRS provides additional contribution room for savers age 50 and older. In 2027, the 401(k) catch-up contribution is $7,500 on top of the standard $25,500 limit, for a total of $31,000. IRA catch-up contributions add $1,000 to the standard $7,000 limit. HSA catch-up for those 55+ adds another $1,000. Combined with employer matching, a 50-year-old couple can potentially shelter $80,000 or more per year in tax-advantaged accounts.

Most financial advice focuses on investment returns, but the variable you control most directly is your savings rate. Moving from a 10% savings rate to a 30% savings rate has a dramatically larger impact on your retirement timeline than chasing an extra 2% of investment return. A household earning $120,000 that increases from 10% to 30% savings — a shift of $24,000 per year — adds roughly $600,000 to their retirement balance over 15 years (assuming 7% average returns).

The FI community's core insight is that savings rate is the primary driver of financial independence. At a 50% savings rate, you can reach FI in roughly 17 years regardless of income level. At 60%, it compresses to about 12 years. At 70%, you are looking at under 10 years. These numbers are independent of salary — they depend only on the ratio of savings to spending.

The average American contributes 4.6% of salary to their 401(k), receives a 3-4% employer match, and saves little outside of that. FIRE-path savers typically max every available tax-advantaged account, maintain savings rates of 40-60%, invest in low-cost index funds, and direct overflow savings into taxable brokerage accounts. The result: FIRE savers in their 40s commonly have $500,000 to $1.5 million in total investable assets — 5 to 10 times the national median for their age group. The difference is not income; many FIRE success stories come from median-income households that simply saved aggressively and avoided lifestyle inflation.

Your savings rate matters more than returns. See where you are.

If you are 40 with $50,000 saved and feeling behind, shifting from a 10% savings rate to a 40% savings rate on a $100,000 income adds $30,000 per year to your investment accounts. At 7% average returns, that alone grows to over $950,000 in 15 years — before counting the $50,000 you already have. Starting late is not ideal, but a high savings rate compresses the timeline dramatically.

Add up every 401(k), IRA, Roth IRA, HSA, and other retirement account balance. Include employer-sponsored plans from previous jobs — many people have orphaned 401(k) accounts they have forgotten about. Exclude your home equity and Social Security for now.

Use the age-bracket tables above to see where you stand. If you are above the median, you are ahead of most Americans your age. If you are below, calculate exactly how far behind and what it would take to catch up.

Most employers allow you to change your 401(k) contribution rate at any time. Increasing by 2% of salary is small enough that you will barely notice the paycheck reduction, but it compounds dramatically over time. Repeat this increase every six months until you are maxing out your 401(k).

Roughly one in four employees leaves free employer match money on the table. If your employer matches 50% of contributions up to 6% of salary, you need to contribute at least 6% to capture the full match. This is an instant 50% return on your money — no investment can beat it.

A Roth IRA provides tax-free growth and tax-free withdrawals in retirement, with no required minimum distributions. The 2026 limit is $7,000 ($8,000 if 50+). If your income exceeds the Roth limits, use the backdoor Roth conversion strategy to contribute indirectly.

Fidelity recommends having 1x your annual salary saved by age 30. For someone earning $55,000, that means $55,000 in retirement accounts. The FI community targets higher — $50,000 to $100,000 by 30 is common among aggressive savers. The national median for under-35 is only $13,000, so if you have more than that, you are already ahead of most peers.

The average is pulled upward by a small percentage of very high-balance accounts. If nine people have $10,000 saved and one person has $1,000,000, the average is $109,000 but the median is $10,000. The median gives a far more accurate picture of what a typical American has saved. Always compare yourself to the median, not the average.

Yes — employer matching contributions are part of your retirement savings balance. In a typical arrangement, an employer matches 50% of your contributions up to 6% of salary. On a $75,000 salary, that adds $2,250 per year in free money. Over a 30-year career at 7% returns, that match alone grows to roughly $213,000.

Generally no. While your home is part of your net worth, it is not liquid retirement savings you can draw from to cover living expenses. You would need to sell or reverse-mortgage your home to access that equity. Retirement planning should focus on investable assets — accounts you can convert to income without selling your primary residence.

A common guideline is 10-12x your pre-retirement income. For a household earning $100,000, that means $1,000,000 to $1,200,000 in retirement savings. The 4% rule suggests you can withdraw 4% of your portfolio annually with a high probability of not running out over 30 years — so $1 million supports roughly $40,000 per year in withdrawals.

It is never too late, but the urgency increases with age. A 40-year-old saving $20,000 per year at 7% returns will accumulate roughly $1 million by age 65. A 50-year-old has access to catch-up contributions ($7,500 extra in a 401(k)) and can still build $400,000 to $600,000 in 15 years with aggressive saving. The key is maximizing savings rate immediately rather than trying to make up ground through risky investments.

The average retirement savings benchmarks are useful directional guides, but they should not define your target. Most Americans are dramatically undersaved — the median 401(k) balance at retirement age is under $75,000, which supports only about $2,860 per year in withdrawals using the 4% rule. That is not a retirement plan; it is a supplement to Social Security at best. The FI community takes a fundamentally different approach: define your actual annual spending, multiply by 25, and work backward to a savings rate that gets you there. Whether your number is $750,000 or $3 million, the path is the same — maximize tax-advantaged accounts, invest in low-cost index funds, maintain a high savings rate, and let compound growth do the heavy lifting. If you are behind the benchmarks, the single most impactful action is increasing your savings rate, not chasing higher returns.

#9363. Latest Analysis: Circumcision Boosts Men’s Sexual Function

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted October 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

Circumcision is controversial, sexually and psychologically.

It involves surgical removal of the foreskin, the skin that covers the head (glans) of the penis. The foreskin contains touch-sensitive nerves. By removing them, circumcision opponents insist that it must reduce the penis’ sexual sensitivity and impair men’s pleasure. On Reddit and other Internet forums, opponents have denounced circumcision as barbarous, unfair to male infants, and physically and psychologically harmful.

Supporters counter that the vast majority of erotically sensitive nerve endings are located in the glans, not the foreskin, and that the procedure does not compromise men’s sexual function or pleasure. Recently, Turkish researchers analyzed 15 studies of circumcision and found that far from impairing men sexually, it enhances men’s sexual function.

The investigators conducted a meta-analysis of 15 previously published studies. Meta-analysis is a standard statistical technique that allows the results of small studies to be combined as if they’d all been one large trial. Study size is important. The larger the study population, the more likely the results are to reflect reality. The 15 studies involved 14,737 men, a number that lends credibility to the findings. The meta-analysis showed that, compared with men with intact foreskins, those who were circumcised reported greater sexual satisfaction (p < 0.001), improved erection function (p = 0.002), less pain during intercourse (p = 0.03), and fewer orgasm difficulties (p = 0.01) (Karaahmet and Lalaeh, 2025).

The researchers evaluated 15 studies, but many more have been conducted. How did they select those 15? They used the World Health Organization’s (WHO) guidelines for grading research rigor and chose only the most credible studies, which is important as many studies of circumcision’s sexual impact have been biased either for or against the procedure.

These reports don’t inspire much confidence.

Circumcision reduces the risk of AIDS (below). Several studies have involved before-and-after surveys of African men circumcised as adults to reduce AIDS risk:

But these studies are also problematic. When they were conducted, AIDS was epidemic in Africa, and many participants feared for their lives. Researchers reassured them that circumcision had no sexual downsides. Critics charged that circumcised subjects felt so relieved to have their AIDS risk reduced that they parroted back what the researchers had told them—that circumcision has no sexual impact.

Using WHO guidelines, the authors of the new report excluded many studies, both pro and con, such as those just mentioned, and included only the most methodologically rigorous studies, which showed that circumcision causes no discernible sexual impairment.

Worldwide, one-third of men are circumcised. Judaism and Islam require it, so in Israel and across the Muslim world, the practice is virtually universal. Circumcision is also popular in the U.S. and Asia, but less so in Europe, Latin America, and non-Muslim Africa.

Jews and Muslims have circumcised boys for centuries. During the 19th century, the practice spread to Christians who believed—mistakenly—that it prevented masturbation. Circumcision is not medically necessary, but it offers health benefits in several areas:

These findings have prompted some Jews and Muslims to claim their faiths were medically prescient and required circumcision for health reasons. But theologians of both religions insist that the practice has always been an act of faith and so its medical benefits, while welcome, are coincidental.

For the vast majority of men, the controversy over circumcision and sexual function is moot. They’re either circumcised or not, and if so, the vast majority have lived that way since infancy and have no way to compare their sexual sensitivity before and after the procedure.

If you’re intact and want to believe you have superior erotic sensitivity, you’re free to feel smug. But the weight of the evidence shows that circumcision does not impair sexual function, and that circumcised men have no reason to fear they’re missing out on erotic pleasure and satisfaction.

Karaahmet, AY and SS Lalaeh. “The Influence of Circumcision on Male Sexual Function: A Meta-Analysis of Satisfaction, Erectile Function, and Dyspareunia,” Journal of Sex and Marital Therapy (2025) 51:551. Doi: 10.1080/0092623X.2025.2499141

Armagan, A. et al. “Circumcision During the Phallic Period: Does It Affect the Psychosexual Functions in Adulthood?" Andrologia (2014) 46:254.

Bollinger, D., and R.S. Van Howe. “Alexithymia and Circumcision Trauma: A Preliminary Investigation,” International Journal of Men’s Health (2011) 10:184.

Bossio, J.A. et al. “Examining Penile Sensitivity in Neonatally Circumcised and Intact Men Using Quantitative Sensory Testing,” Journal of Urology (2016) 195:1848.

Bronselaer, G.A. et al. “Male Circumcision Decreases Penile Sensitivity As Measured in a Large Cohort,” BJU International (2013) 111:820.

Cortes-Gonzalez, J.R. et al. “Does Circumcision Affect Male’s Perception of Sexual Satisfaction?” Arch. Esp. Urol. (2009) 62:733.

Dias, J. et al. “Adult Circumcision and Male Sexual Health: A Retrospective Analysis,” Andrologia (2014) 46:459.

Homfray, V. et al. “Examining the Association Between Male Circumcision and Sexual Function: Evidence from a British Probability Survey,” AIDS (2015) 29:1411.

Hoschke, B. et al. “Male Circumcision Is Not Associated with an Increased Prevalence of Erectile Dysfunction: Results of the Cottbus 10,000 Men Survey,” Der Urologe (2013) 52:562.

Kigozi, G. et al. “The Effect of Male Circumcision on Sexual Satisfaction and Function: Results from a Randomized Trial of Male Circumcision for Human Immunodeficiency Virus Prevention in Rakai, Uganda,” BJU [formerly British Journal of Urology] (2008) 101:65. Doi:10.1111/j.1464-410X.2007.07369.x

Krieger, J.N. et al. “Adult Male Circumcision: Effects on Sexual Function and Satisfaction in Kisumu, Kenya,” Journal of Sexual Medicine (2008) 5:2610.

Shabanzadeh, D.M. et al. “Male Circumcision Does Not Result in Inferior Perceived Male Sexual Function: A Systematic Review,” Danish Medical Journal (2016) 63:pii:A5245.

#9362. What Poetry Can Teach Us About Wonder: An Interview With Maya C. Popa

The most trusted resource for mindfulness and meditation.

An interview with poet Maya C. Popa on attention, uncertainty, and the art of remaining curious.

We often associate wonder with extraordinary experiences, moments of beauty or awe that stop us in our tracks. But what if wonder is also a way of paying attention, one that invites us to question what we think we know and remain open to what we cannot immediately understand?

Poetry offers a particular way of exploring this possibility. It asks us to slow down, look more closely, and make room for ambiguity, uncertainty, and experiences that resist easy explanation. In doing so, poetry may have something to teach us about presence, curiosity, and our capacity to find meaning in the world around us.

What if wonder is a way of paying attention that invites us to question what we think we know and remain open to what we cannot immediately understand?

Poet Maya C. Popa has spent years exploring wonder through her doctoral research and her creative work. Her collection Wound Is the Origin of Wonder examines wonder beyond beauty and astonishment, while her newest collection, If You Love That Lady, explores the ways attention and experience can challenge our assumptions. In this conversation, Popa reflects on the relationship between poetry and mindfulness, the value of questioning our perceptions, and how cultivating wonder might deepen our connection to the world around us.

As a fellow graduate of NYU’s Creative Writing Program, I’ve had the opportunity to work with Maya over the past several years and follow the evolution of her writing. The author of three poetry collections and three chapbooks, and founder of the Conscious Writers Collective, she has devoted much of her creative and scholarly life to exploring how wonder shapes our  experience of the world.

Angela Stubbs: You’ve spent years exploring wonder both as a scholar and as a poet. Having lived with the subject for so long, how has your understanding of it changed??

Maya C. Popa: I’ve become more sensitive to how “wonder” is used conversationally, often as a substitute for admiration, surprise, or delight. It’s understandable, of course, because wonder can share qualities with the sublime or awe-inspiring. But my PhD focused specifically on the idea that wonder leads us to ask questions, which is where I think its true power lies.

My intention was to study wonder not merely through an aesthetic or critical lens, but as a fundamental human aptitude.

If we look at wonder’s etymology, it’s clear it’s not a tidy, straightforward, or uncomplicated experience. It derives from the Old English wundor, which some scholars have suggested may be related to German wunde or wound. The noun form means a surpassing or breach of the mind’s faculties, while the verb form means to demonstrate a state of admiration or astonishment, or to search for understanding or meaning. “The verb wonder,” writes scholar Daniel Fusch, “indicates an emotional response to a marvelous incident; the noun wonder indicates both the name for that response and the marvelous incident that provoked it…That is, at the sight of a wonder, we wonder; such are the beautiful complications of the English language.”

My intention was to study wonder not merely through an aesthetic or critical lens, but as a fundamental human aptitude that we could cultivate that ultimately serves as a vehicle for curiosity and empathy. Of course, I also believe it’s vitally important to live in a state of appreciation and gratitude, but wonder’s stakes and demands are psychically fascinating and deserve to be considered closely by teasing out these semantic distinctions. This allows us to fully own the power of wonder, not just treat it as another modern buzzword.

Angela Stubbs: You’ve spoken before about wonder as involving both knowing and not knowing. In the opening poem of If You Love That Lady, “At the Entrance of a Love Poem, I Hesitate,” there’s a sense that arriving at an answer can actually end the inquiry. What interests you about keeping a question alive? Is there something poetry allows us to experience by resisting the impulse to resolve or explain too quickly?

Maya C. Popa: Poems unearth and discover as they go; they are, as our wonderful Nobel Laureate Anne Carson suggests, “an action of the mind captured on a page…a movement of yourself through a thought, through an activity of thinking.” Wonder catalyzes the poetic impulse. I do think it provokes a generative restlessness that naturally seeks its shape in language.

I also believe that wonder can be passed from writer to reader.

I also believe that wonder can be passed from writer to reader. As Peter de Bolla suggests in his study of aesthetic experience, literary works of art are produced through the activity of reading. It makes sense—as we read, we’re responding in our heads as we metabolize it. Reading is inherently interactive, especially for writers.

So, to answer the question more directly, I absolutely believe in the value of keeping the question alive, and I think part of our sense of aliveness comes from that feeling of ongoing inquiry into life. Rilke advised the young poet to “Be patient toward all that is unsolved in your heart and try to love the questions themselves.” We can witness the results of our need for immediate resolution, certainty, and shortcuts everywhere in our culture. It’s at the heart of some of our greatest concerns (artificial intelligence, GLP-1s, etc.). There are an increasing number of ways around critical thinking. Sitting with, even taking as much enjoyment in the question as the solution, feels like an essential part of thinking and writing to me.

In the case of the opening poem, I wanted to begin with a self-interrogation that acknowledged the recurrence of love poems throughout history, and the ways that the beloved always seems to be situated at a distance, inviting the poet to write towards them to close the gap. Then there’s the notion, also helpfully introduced by Anne Carson, that desire requires a gap. So, this collection reflects a great deal on these questions.

I always think of Lucille Clifton saying that poems come out of wonder, not out of knowing.

Angela Stubbs: Throughout this collection, perceptions are revised: a mouse becomes a wren, a hawk moth is mistaken for a hummingbird. Do you see wonder as a willingness to discover that our first perceptions, or the stories we tell ourselves, are incomplete? Does this relate, in some way, to the writing process, which requires a similar receptivity? How do you know when to direct a poem and when to follow what it is becoming?

Maya C. Popa: I always think of Lucille Clifton saying that poems come out of wonder, not out of knowing. I value that kind of mental flexibility and capacity to revise one’s thinking or perception instead of stagnating or atrophying around a belief. That openness and capacity to evaluate and reevaluate as needed is invaluable to poets, who do this regularly throughout the process of revising. I certainly wanted to pay attention to this capacity when I noticed it in myself and deliver it on the page as precisely as I could. As a poet, I often feel I’m acting both as the lightning and the bottle that captures it at the same time.

Practically, I have to listen very closely for the deeper and more interesting questions beneath the surface of my writing as I go. What drove me to the page may not be what interests me by the end of many drafts. All of this requires me to set my ego to the side and be ruthlessly honest when something is not working, either because it isn’t rigorous or precise enough in its thinking, or it hasn’t yet found its music.

It’s rare that I’ll have a poem come together over only a handful of drafts; it’s more likely that I’m working on several poems over the course of a year or two, and many I will never share.

This requires me not to know for a lot of the time, and then, as I discover and distill what I’m doing, to make that discovery legible first to myself, and then hopefully to the reader. This takes revision in layers over many months or years. That is about the time it takes for me to really understand my own sound-sense on the page. It’s rare that I’ll have a poem come together over only a handful of drafts; it’s more likely that I’m working on several poems over the course of a year or two, and many I will never share.

Angela Stubbs: In “February Clear,” you turn from looking at the natural world toward the possibility that looking itself can change us. What is the difference, for you, between merely seeing something and giving it the kind of attention that might actually alter the person who is looking?

Maya C. Popa: I always think of the adage that we see things not as they are, but as we are. I also think that we often show up with our psyches in 12 different places at once. How often are we thinking of the thing we have to do next, the irritating conversations that we just had, what other people are doing on the internet, etc? It’s hard to stay in our own lane, and in our own moment.

[A]ttention and importance are also relayed and understood through language. If ours is significantly limited, how can we advocate for the natural world?

In that poem, I was trying to capture the experience of looking and really seeing, and acknowledging how often that isn’t the case. As someone who did not grow up with an agrarian vernacular, I also acknowledge that while my ancestors might have looked at green spaces and immediately conjured a palette of words for what they noticed, I can only name a handful of any landscape’s features. And those are mostly the obvious things: the hills, the grass, the rocks. I can’t name the kind of tree or type of grass. And this matters, because attention and importance are also relayed and understood through language. If ours is significantly limited, how can we advocate for the natural world? My friend, the extraordinary naturalist Robert Macfarlane, says that “we will not save what we do not love, and we rarely love what we cannot name.”

Angela Stubbs: We often talk about “cultivating wonder,” particularly in mindfulness and contemplative spaces, as though wonder were something we could deliberately produce. After studying and writing about it for so many years, do you think wonder itself can be cultivated, or can we only cultivate the attention, openness, and receptivity that allow us to recognize it when it appears?

If we treat wonder as being purely positive, as being in constant admiration, we will so often fall prey to our moods, which will make it hard or make it feel forced.

Maya C. Popa: I think we absolutely can and should cultivate a sense of wonder. But if we come back to its purpose as being partially to drive us to ask questions, not just to admire, I think we’re closer to the thing that actually counts, which is not taking things for granted. If we treat wonder as being purely positive, as being in constant admiration, we will so often fall prey to our moods, which will make it hard or make it feel forced.

Cultivating wonder initially involves paying attention a bit more deliberately than we usually would, before it becomes a kind of natural orientation. It’s slightly different from a gratitude practice, although it also gets us out of our sense of routine and shows us what is quite unlikely, the “marvelous singularity” of our human experience.

Rachel Carson said that “the more clearly we can focus our attention on the wonders and realities of the universe about us, the less taste we shall have for the destruction of our race,” and I stand by her thinking that wonder and humility are what safeguard us from egregious destruction. If we can wonder at the unlikeliness and distinctiveness of a human life, then we’re less likely to turn to violence. The more we develop our capacity to wonder, the greater our art, certainly, and the greater the hope that we will see our interconnectedness and protect and value each other.

Angela Stubbs is the founder of Pitch Perfect Media, a PR company dedicated to amplifying the voices of women and visionaries shaping culture and change. She holds dual MFAs in Creative Writing—one in Fiction from the Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics at Naropa University, and one in Poetry from the Creative Writing Program at NYU Paris—where her studies in contemplative education and poetics deepened her meditation practice. Angela leads heart-centered meditation offerings in Los Angeles and is currently at work on a poetry manuscript exploring memory, surrender, and the art of letting go.

#9361. When It Makes Sense To “Block” The Main Thread

I Code. I Write. Meme Rules. Ok, but seriously, I’m a web and mobile developer who writes a lot. In my spare time, I like to build products that would … More about Victor ↬

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

We’ve all heard of the sacred rule in modern web development, the rule never to be broken. The rule of “Never block the main thread.”

You almost can’t miss it as a web developer; it’s in almost every performance guide, and to be fair, it is good advice. We all know the browser’s main thread is single-threaded, meaning it can only do one thing at a time.

Plus, as we know, the main thread isn’t ours alone; we share it with the browser’s rendering engine, input handlers, and other critical tasks. As a result, the less time we hold onto the main thread, the more responsive an app feels. That leads us to share tasks with background workers as we’ve convinced ourselves there should be a hard line between the UI and any computation, and that line shouldn’t be crossed.

And that is what a “recommended” architecture looks like.

But I dare say that *sometimes*, moving the data to a worker is slower than just letting the main thread do the work.

I found this out a few months ago while building a Chrome extension with screenshotting features called Fastary. I kept finding a latency of about 2 to 3 seconds in all my testing, even after using an Offscreen Document (a background process in Chrome extensions) to handle the canvas operations. A screenshot task should feel instant without lag, after all.

It is quite ironic that by reflex, we move work away from the main thread to avoid freezing the UI, but sometimes the act of moving that work (e.g., serializing, copying, and deserializing) can also freeze the UI. And sometimes the recommended approach of letting the background do the work can be slower than just doing the work on the main thread.

Meet Smashing Workshops on front-end, design & UX, with practical takeaways, live sessions, video recordings and a friendly Q&A. With Brad Frost, Stéph Walter and so many others.

To put things in perspective, let’s understand why we isolate browser contexts and how they communicate with each other, with emphasis on the communication part.

A browser is more than a single environment. Different environments are running at the same time, each having its own memory space, what it can access, and rules:

Each one of these is isolated from the others. A web worker or background script lives in a different memory space from the main thread. They cannot just reach and read each other’s variables or logic, and this is known as the “shared-nothing” architecture.

How do these isolated environments communicate? They explicitly message each other back and forth using APIs, like postMessage().

postMessage() tells the browser to take a piece of data and deliver it to the context that requested it. But to do this, the browser relies on the Structured Clone Algorithm (SCA).

You’re probably familiar with JSON.stringify(). SCA is similar, but much stronger and smarter. In its simplest form, SCA is a deep, recursive copy operation, i.e., cloning. It walks through the entire data structure it is given, clones every single value, serializes it into a transportable format, ships those bytes to the target contexts, and then reconstructs the original object on the receiving side.

SCA is fast, or maybe fast-ish… For a small regular config object like {theme: "dark"}, it is imperceptible; you don’t even notice it. The story changes, however, when dealing with heavy data because the SCA is a synchronous blocking O(n) operation, i.e., the cost increases linearly with the size of your data.

Let’s put that into perspective. A user clicks a button, and internally, an 8MB image payload is sent to a background worker for processing. When you call postMessage(), the main thread must immediately stop what it is doing to run this serialization and copying process.

I’m sure some of you are already thinking, “Why not just use Transferable objects?” And that is a valid point. Let’s talk about that.

Developers who really pursue ultra-high-performance web apps usually use Transferable objects (e.g., ArrayBuffer, ImageBitmap, or MessagePort) to bypass the Structured Clone Algorithm. This is because when you transfer an object, you’re not making a copy (like SCM). Instead, the browser switches ownership of the data from one context to another.

The browser performs a hand-off whereby the sending context loses access to the data instantly, and the receiving context takes full control. It is actually insanely fast. According to Chrome Developers’ benchmark, transferring a massive 32MB ArrayBuffer can take under 7ms, compared to about 300ms when cloning with SCM. That’s a 43x speed boost.

But like all good things, there are downsides. To name a few:

So, as far as my screenshot extension went, Transferable objects were not an option.

Why do we even bother isolating contexts at all? Why not just leave it all to the main thread?

Offloading long-running CPU tasks to a background thread is absolutely the right thing to do. The browser needs to paint a new frame every 16.6ms to keep things fluid; that means any task that takes >50ms is generally considered “long”. Offloading to the background is absolutely the right thing to do.

The issue, however, is that we’ve turned this “never block the main thread” into an absolute rule, without asking is this task expensive to process or expensive to move?

I have come to realize now that the rule is less “never block the main thread” than “never block the main thread for too long.”

My goal with the Fastary extension was to make it feel like a native app, running as smoothly and instantly as you would expect a native app to.

As you already know, I took the recommended approach to use the Offscreen Document to handle DOM work in the background. But to my surprise, that took a different turn.

The Offscreen Document API is a clear winner. You create a hidden, undisplayed document that runs entirely in the background. It has a DOM and supports Canvas. For example, if I want to crop a screenshot, stitch multiple screenshots together, perform heavy image manipulation, or add a watermark, Offscreen Document was made for that.

Turns out that was not the best approach. This was my architecture:

But when I tested it, the screenshot didn’t feel instant. As I said earlier, there was a consistent 2–3 second lag.

I figured out that when captureVisibleTab() takes a screenshot, it returns a Base64 URL string, and on a standard 1080p screen, that string could be approximately 1MB or more, depending on how detailed the image is. It gets even more interesting on modern Retina displays (e.g., MacBooks) as they tend to automatically double the image’s size by default.

Keep in mind that since the image payload could be doubled and extension messaging relies on JSON serialization (as of this writing), we potentially deal with massive synchronous communication that costs an entire round trip.

The image string data is JSON-serialized at least twice: once when going into the Offscreen Document and once coming back out with the processed results to the background worker. The actual image processing (cropping) done inside the Offscreen Document was fast, no doubt, but I can’t say the same about the transfer overhead.

As if the latency itself wasn’t enough, I noticed a rather subtle bug — which, now that I think of it, was more of my ignorance. After a screenshot was taken, the crop result was completely off in a way that either weirdly scaled the image or resulted in incorrect coordinates.

It turns out that when a user selects a region to crop, the content script gets the box coordinates using getBoundingClientRect(), which is measured in CSS pixels; this is what the DOM uses. But when the screenshot is captured natively in Chrome, the browser doesn’t crop it automatically; it instead uses the physical hardware pixels to get the full screen capture. And the browser uses devicePixelRatio (DPR) to know how many physical pixels should represent one CSS pixel. Basically, if a user on a Retinal display (DPR = 2) highlights an area of 400x300 CSS pixels, the actual captured image area is 800x600 physical pixels.

For an accurate crop, I needed to apply these two different measurement systems with the right DPR, i.e., scale the crop coordinates by the DPR. But remember, Offscreen Documents have no physical display. Processing any image would have a default DPR equal to 1. To fix this, I would have to capture the exact devicePixelRatio from the active tab, serialize it, pass it alongside the image payload, and manually do the scaling math inside the Offscreen Document. The complexity starts to compound.

What if I broke the golden rule and did the work on the main thread instead?

Some developers will argue that UI tasks are the only things that should run on the main thread, but I don’t fully agree with that. Personally, I believe that user explicitly-invoked actions that need immediate results can sometimes get a solid pass to run on the main thread, provided the work is incredibly fast (e.g., 1s).

That’s what I did: scrap out the Offscreen Document and reengineer the logic. Instead of:

…I decided to run the whole image processing in the active tab:

This approach completely clears out multiple context hops and round trips that JSON serialization requires. The only cross-context transfer involves sending the data URL from the background to the content script.

The Retina DPI issue essentially solved itself, as the content script runs directly inside the real, active browser tab because it knows the monitor’s real devicePixelRatio.

But there’s an elephant in the room that you may have noticed.

Sure, the image is now processed on the main thread, and the background manipulates the canvas in the active tab. I could technically be blocking the main thread. That’s where I amended the “no blocking the main thread” rule to “no blocking the main thread for too long.” In this specific case, at least, blocking the main thread for a task the user requests for approximately one second is justifiable. It works conversely as well: maybe don’t isolate processes if the data transfer cost is greater than the processing cost.

I’ve boiled it down to a mental model that depends on whether the task is:

These are tasks where the primary cost is computation and not the size of the data itself. These are tasks where most of the time is spent on doing calculations or heavy transformations, e.g., image compression, audio profiling, physics simulation, etc.

The transfer cost for these tasks is minuscule compared to the actual work.

These tasks are the exact opposite. These tasks are only expensive because of the size. The processing time is almost insignificant, but the data is expensive to transport, e.g., image cropping, filtering an array, shallow copy, etc.

In my specific case, offloading the task to the background falls mostly into negative-sum efficiency. If we are talking about moving megabytes of data to perform a 50ms operation, there is no benefit to offloading it to the background.

Looking at this, if the “background processing time” is the most dominant task in your operation, then isolation is the clear winner. But if serialization, plus deserialization, plus transit exceeds that cost, then there’s no need to isolate things.

And if you can’t figure out if the task is CPU-heavy or data-heavy, it certainly doesn’t hurt to measure it, for example, using performance.mark() and performance.measure() around postMessage calls to profile the transfer cost.

#9360. How to Cope With Loneliness: 5 Mindfulness Practices to Feel More Connected

The most trusted resource for mindfulness and meditation.

Feeling lonely isn't a personal failing, and you don't have to transform your social life overnight in order to feel more connected. Try these five gentle mindfulness practices.

I live in a rural area, about four miles from my nearest neighbor. My husband works away on a two-weeks-on, two-weeks-off rotation, which is fairly common where I live. The community is widely scattered, you need a car to get almost anywhere, and there isn’t a great deal of interaction between neighbors. In fact, I suspect many people don’t even know who lives closest to them.

But I want to make something clear: I’m not generally a lonely person.

Loneliness doesn’t only find people with empty calendars or empty houses. It looks different for everyone.

At school, I was labeled a “loner.” I’ve never had a large circle of friends, preferring instead the company of two or three close ones. Those friendships have lasted through the years and many birthdays. Two of my closest friends live in the UK, and we keep in touch through online chats, time difference and all.

#9359. New contemporary art centre coming to University of California, San Diego

Strauss Family Gallery, University of California, San Diego Photo: Pablo Mason, courtesy UC San Diego

The University of California, San Diego will open a 12,000-sq.-ft contemporary art space on its campus in spring 2027. Housed in the university’s new Triton Center, the Strauss Family Gallery will include four indoor exhibition spaces and an outdoor sculpture terrace. Free and open to the public, the Strauss will host exhibitions, commissions, artist residencies and public programmes that encourage collaboration between artists and UC San Diego researchers and scholars.

Jessica Berlanga Taylor, UC San Diego’s chief campus curator, tells The Art Newspaper that the university is aware of the challenges other San Diego cultural institutions are facing and believes investing in art and culture is essential. "The Strauss represents a long-term commitment that the university is making to contemporary art and sees it as an integral part of the university's intellectual and public life," she says.

In 2023, the local philanthropists Matthew and Iris Strauss gave more than 100 works form their art collection to UC San Diego. (Matthew, who made his money in real estate, died the following year.) Represented artists in the gift include Carrie Mae Weems, Fred Wilson, Zhang Huan and Sabine Moritz.

The Strauss’s new David and Claire Guggenheim Gallery will serve as the public entrance and a space for exhibitions, gatherings and an artist-in-residence programme focused on digital artists, while the two-story Gray Box will accommodate large-scale sculpture, moving-image installations and performances.

The 3,043-sq.-ft Black Box will be equipped for immersive video, sound, sculpture and performance; and the White Cube will provide a more conventional gallery setting for works from the Strauss Family Foundation, travelling exhibitions and collaborations with collections in San Diego and beyond.

Taylor calls the Strauss the first "ground-up museum" at UC San Diego. Pointing to existing spaces on campus like the Mandeville Art Gallery (open for nearly 60 years) and a black-box theatre in the music department, she says the Strauss will strive to be part of the landscape of both the campus and San Diego at large. But the Strauss will play a unique role—with commissions, curatorial research and exhibitions in collaboration with artists from across the globe.

UC San Diego’s Stuart Collection, which includes sculptures installed across campus, has already established a public art presence at the university. The Strauss will now give artists a dedicated space for exhibitions, commissions and research.

“We’re connecting art inside with art outside now with the Strauss and the Stuart Collection, but we also want to distinguish very clearly what Stuart is about and what the Strauss will achieve," Taylor says. "The Strauss is very much about perception and experience, but it’s also about expanding our ways of knowing and presenting different forms of knowledge that you wouldn’t necessarily encounter in the classroom."

Taylor's greater vision is to engage the community through public programming and student involvement. The Strauss plans to engage both established and emerging artists, particularly in the digital space, and support the development of their work. "We're looking at how we can bring artistic inquiry into university teaching and research," Taylor says.

This could include incorporating exhibitions and artistic methodologies into existing courses, giving students opportunities to participate in curatorial research and creative projects, and developing collaborations across the university. Taylor points to potential partnerships with UC San Diego’s Qualcomm Institute, the Interdisciplinary Computing and the Arts programme, the Scripps Institution of Oceanography and the Goeddel Family Technology Sandbox as examples of the range of possibilities.

"We see the Strauss as more of a platform than a container for a collection," Taylor says. "We do have a collection, but our goal is to be a platform for research and critical inquiry—and for challenging assumptions."

#9358. Finding the Tailwinds That Help Us Move Forward

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted October 15, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

So often, our attention gravitates toward what is wrong, challenging, or missing. Yet when we focus solely on what is not working, we lose sight of the things that are helping us along.

I find it helpful to think about the headwinds and tailwinds moving through our lives.

Headwinds are the pressures, stressors, and challenges that push against us. They are the things coming at us, demanding our attention, threatening to knock us off course, or making it harder to move in the direction we want to go. Some are temporary, while others are part of circumstances we cannot quickly change. Tailwinds are the forces supporting us from behind and within. They include our strengths, skills, relationships, routines, experiences, and values that help us keep going. They may not remove the headwinds, but they can help us meet them with greater support and perspective.

In Stress Wisely, I explore wellness through eight interconnected dimensions: physical, emotional, intellectual, social, environmental, occupational, financial, and spiritual. Each offers a different lens through which we're able to notice what is hindering us, what is helping us, and where we might find room for growth.

Wellness is an ongoing process of understanding what we need, noticing what supports us, and making adjustments as our circumstances change. Perhaps we are not sleeping as well as we would like, feel disconnected from the people we care about, are carrying financial stress, or have lost touch with the activities that give our lives meaning. These concerns deserve our attention, and sometimes they call for change, additional support, or a closer look at what is possible within our circumstances. At the same time, my gentle invitation is to ask ourselves: What is already working for me here?

It is easy to focus on what our bodies are not able to do or what we wish we could change, but we can also appreciate what they help us experience and what we are doing to care for them. Perhaps a 30-minute walk every day helps you clear your mind, a consistent bedtime is allowing you to show up with better energy, or you've learned to recognize when you are running on empty and need to slow down. These everyday choices matter.

If you thought of your body as a vehicle carrying you through life, what is helping you take good care of it and keep it going?

Emotional wellness is about learning to recognize our feelings and respond to them with greater understanding instead of ignoring them or expecting ourselves to push through them. One tailwind may be your growing ability to name what you are feeling. Maybe you give yourself 90 seconds to sit with an emotion and let it move through you, find comfort in a creative outlet, or reach out to a trusted person rather than carrying everything alone. These are ways of making room for our emotions as we navigate the hard parts.

What helps you process your feelings and meet yourself with a little more compassion?

We learn through curiosity, reflection, conversation, and experience. Each and every one of us has skills we've developed over time, mistakes we've learned from, and different perspectives we've opened ourselves up to that have broadened our thinking.

Thinking of a particular area in your life, what have you learned, figured out, or become more capable of doing?

We are not meant to navigate life alone. A friend who checks in, a colleague who understands, or a community where we feel we belong can remind us we are supported and valued. We can also notice the strengths we bring to our relationships, such as being a good listener, a thoughtful encourager, or a practical problem-solver. Connection is about the support we receive, but it's also about the ways we contribute to one another.

Who helps you feel safe, seen, and supported? What do you bring to the relationships that matter to you?

Our surroundings can influence how we feel and move through our days. We can't always change our environment, but we can notice the places that bring a little ease. Maybe it's a favourite park bench, a sunny spot by your living room window, or a calm corner where you can collect your thoughts. Creating and spending time in hope-filled havens that offer comfort and inspiration can make a difference.

Which places help you feel more settled, connected, or at ease?

Our contributions extend beyond paid work to include caregiving, parenting, volunteering, and the many responsibilities that make up our days. When the demands feel relentless, we may overlook the care we bring to our work, the problems we have solved, or the difference we make in the lives of others. A tailwind might be recognizing a task you carry out that makes someone else's day easier, setting a boundary around email, asking for support, keeping a commitment that reflects your values, or celebrating the small wins.

Where do you find meaning in the work you get to do, and what helps you do it in a sustainable way?

When financial pressures are weighing on us, it can be hard to see what we're doing well and what is working for us. Recognizing what's helping us doesn't mean pretending those worries aren't real. Perhaps you have become more aware of your spending, started a conversation you've been avoiding, learned something about budgeting, or reached out to understand your options.

What is helping you feel more informed, supported, or prepared when it comes to your resources?

Spiritual wellness can be rooted in faith, and it can also be found in our values, sense of purpose, and connection to something larger than ourselves. Noticing the moments that remind us of what matters most can help us make choices that reflect it. Maybe it's spending time in nature, being of service, a prayer practice or familiar ritual, or making time for the people and causes you care about.

When do you feel most connected to what matters most to you?

We cannot always choose what life brings our way. Yet even when things feel difficult, we can widen our view so that what is hard is not the only thing we see.

This is where I believe gratitude is one of the mightiest forces we have for living well. It draws our attention to what might otherwise go unnoticed, helping us recognize what is sustaining us today and what we can carry forward into tomorrow.

Hanley-Dafoe, R. (2023). Stress wisely: How to be well in an unwell world. Page Two.

#9357. Elisha Goldstein: A Nourishing Breath Meditation

The most trusted resource for mindfulness and meditation.

The deepest healing occurs when you come to terms with the way things are. This simple awareness of breath practice is an act of self-love and compassion for the moment we find ourselves in.

Mindful breathing often serves as the foundation for meditation practices because your breath is always with you, wherever you are, and it can be used as an anchor to the present moment. In essence, all that’s involved is simply being mindful when you breathe in and out. There is no need to analyze, count, visu­alize, or manipulate the breath in any way. Just breathe normally and naturally and be aware of breathing in and out. There are a few methods you can use to focus on your breath. You can be mindful of your breath in your nose, chest, belly, or even your entire body as it breathes in and out.

With any of these practices, the deepest healing occurs when you come to terms with the way things are.

For dealing with the challenges of stress and anxiety, we sometimes recommend abdominal breath­ing—breathing from the belly, rather than only into the chest—as this can be very calming. However, if another location is preferable, please listen to your own wisdom. Generally speaking, abdominal or belly breathing is the way we all naturally breathe, especially when we’re lying down. To determine if you’re breathing from your abdomen, place your hand on your belly and feel whether it expands as you inhale and contracts as you exhale. If it doesn’t, turn your attention to breathing more deeply and feeling your belly expand and contract with your breath.

An important benefit of abdominal or belly breathing is that it helps moderate irregular breathing patterns, which often arise due to stress or irritation. Anxiety can lead to shallow, rapid, or sporadic breathing and even hyperventilation, and a full-blown panic attack can cause increased shortness of breath, thoughts of losing control, and pains in the chest. By bringing the breath back into the belly, you can help the body return to balance. So when anxiety arises, first acknowledge the feeling, then gently bring attention to the abdomen and practice mindful belly breathing.

Before we begin, we have one final bit of advice: With any of these practices, the deepest healing occurs when you come to terms with the way things are. This might mean simply noticing and acknowledging stress or anxiety rather than falling into old patterns of running away from it. You may discover that by embracing your fear you find your heart.

Do this practice in a relaxing environment without distractions, such as the phone. You can do it either lying down or sitting up, but if you lie down and find yourself falling asleep, try a more upright posture. Bring your full, undivided attention to this practice as you listen or read the following meditation, pausing after each paragraph. You can practice anytime throughout the day, combining this practice with the mindful check-in if you like.

Read and practice the guided meditation script below, pausing after each paragraph. Or listen to the audio practice.
